# The White House's Post-Election Shake-Up: From the Politics Desk

(Fetch tool returned a condensed rendering; text below is as returned.)

## Trump Names Stephen Miller His New Chief of Staff, Replacing Susie Wiles
By Jonathan Allen and Rebecca Shabad

Following Republicans' significant losses in Tuesday's midterm elections, President Donald Trump has appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff. Miller, who previously served as deputy chief of staff, replaces Susie Wiles, who resigned Thursday evening.

Trump announced the transition on Truth Social, with Miller assuming the role Monday. This shift signals Trump's intention to strengthen ties with the MAGA base during his final two years in office.

Miller has architected the administration's mass-deportation campaign. The change from establishment figure Wiles to Miller suggests a more combative approach toward Democrats in Congress.

Steve Bannon, former Trump aide, characterized Miller as someone who "knows the key issues" and will take "immediate control." An unnamed ally told reporters that Miller executes presidential directives decisively: "When the president says, 'Do this,' Stephen will do it, and he'll leave bodies behind doing it."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries responded critically, stating that "Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands" and calling for his removal.

## The Midterms Reveal a Much Larger Slice of the Electorate Is Up for Grabs
Analysis by Kristen Welker

The 2026 midterms demonstrate that swing voters—young, Latino, and disaffected citizens—represent a substantially larger portion of the electorate than previously recognized.

These same voters powered Trump's 2024 victory but swung decisively back to Democrats in 2026, indicating both elections reflected voter rejection of the status quo rather than permanent political realignment.

Pre-election and exit polling reveals these voters believe Trump failed to address rising inflation and reduce costs as promised during his campaign.

Democrats now face the challenge of converting electoral success into legislative achievements while managing internal divisions. Republicans must navigate their disappointing election results and chart a new course forward.

## Additional Top Stories

Jobs Report: The economy added 165,000 jobs in October, a stronger-than-expected figure including apparent AI-related construction and manufacturing positions.

DOJ Investigation: A Trump appointee leading a federal investigation into law enforcement officials involved in prior presidential investigations has resigned.

Legal Challenge: A federal judge temporarily blocked construction on Trump's proposed "Triumphal Arch" following approval by a presidentially appointed planning commission.

Senator's Health: Senator Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) was discharged from the hospital after experiencing what doctors described as a minor hemorrhagic stroke last weekend.
